newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Opposition says French-paid mercenaries in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Opposition says French-paid mercenaries in Zaire.

text.p: A leading Zairean opposition party said on Thursday that some 300 mercenaries paid by France were in Zaire to support President Mobutu Sese Seko's rule and another 700 had been recruited.

The allegation came from the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS) at a news conference in Brussels. Spokeswoman Justine M'Poyo Kasa-Vubu said the mercenaries were from France, Belgium and South Africa.

She said France could no longer afford politically to send its own troops to Zaire and was therefore helping Mobutu set up a mercenary force to fight Laurent Kabila's rebels who control much of the east of the country.

"Paris has accepted to support this action...the French are paying for it," she said. "There are at least 300 mercenaries in Zaire, another 700 have been recruited and are spread over different locations elsewhere."
France denies any involvement with mercenaries, saying it is the victim of a media smear campaign.

The office of President Jacques Chirac has said it had no connection with, or knowledge of, a mercenary force. Cooperation Minister Jacques Godfrain has said there were mercenaries from some European nations in the region but denied any official French involvement.
France backs Mobutu politically but an international arms embargo on Zaire bars any military aid.

The Paris daily Le Monde said on Tuesday that South African, French, Belgian, British, Angolan and Mozambican mercenaries had gathered in eastern Zaire. It said the force numbered between 200 and 300 but was expected to grow rapidly.

But Alain Le Caro, the former security chief at the French presidency who Le Monde said was in Zaire putting together the "White Legion", turned up in Paris and and said he was neither directly nor indirectly involved with soldiers of fortune.
A spokesman for the rebels, who now occupy a 500-km (300-mile) swathe of Zaire along the border with Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi, has also accused Mobutu of bringing in mercenaries.

Kasa-Vubu said they were needed both to fight the rebls and to help Mobutu keep his position. During his 31-year rule Mobutu has on several occasions used mercenaries and foreign troops to put down rebellions.
Kasa-Vubu -- daughter of Zaire's first president Joseph Kasa-Vubu, who was overthrown by Mobutu -- said that France wants to play a role in Mobutu's succession.

Mobutu returned to France on Thursday, to consult doctors about his health, according to Zairean officials. He had flown back to Zaire on December 17 after four months in Switzerland and France for cancer treatment.
"France wants a successor who will be as amenable (to French interests) as Mobutu," Kasa-Vubu said.

She suggested that General Mahele, Zaire's new army chief appointed in mid-December to crush Kabila's rebels, could be a French choice. "If General Mahele does not distance himself from the French, he will be condemned by popular anger," she said.
Kasa-Vubu stopped short of supporting Kabila but said: "He is Zairean and he has the same goals as us: a return to the rule of law and the eradication of dictatorship."
"Kabila has taken to violence, it is the only language Mobutu understands," she said.
